clue.text: Town with dubious Latin charm

indicators.note: dubious letters are suspect and not to be trusted in their order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A town whose charm owes something to questionable Latin mottoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dubious' signals the anagram of LATIN plus CHARM. ALTRINCHAM is a town in Greater Manchester, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Altrincham is a market town near Manchester, so it is one example of a town.

clue.text: It approximates to a cover?

parts.note: a heavy garment worn outside other clothes behaves roughly like a blanket or covering laid over a person

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical description: a long warm garment is, near enough, a cover you wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A long outer garment worn over clothing serves as a wearable covering, so it approximates a cover.

clue.text: Composer providing part of violin passage in piece of music?

definitions.meaning: Frank ... was an English composer and teacher of Benjamin Britten
the raised wooden piece holding the strings above the violin's body
a connecting section linking two themes in a song or movement

explanation.surface: A composer supplying the violin part for a passage in a work.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions joined by 'providing' and 'in': a composer's surname, a violin component and a linking musical passage.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Bridge is a composer; the violin's string support and a transitional musical passage are both called by that same word.

clue.text: Employer's extremes of boastfulness

indicators.note: only the far ends of the word boastfulness are kept, the opening pair and the closing pair, and its middle stretch is dropped

explanation.surface: A manager known for bragging at both ends of the scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes of' keeps the first two and last two letters of BOASTFULNESS, BO and SS; the 's after 'Employer' is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is the person who hires and directs staff, the one paying wages.

clue.text: Cocktail getting Red Army drunk

parts.note: something red as blood can be called bloody

indicators.note: drunk letters are tipsy and stagger out of order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Soldiers of the Red Army getting drunk on cocktails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Army' reads as one Soviet phrase, but RED gives BLOODY and 'drunk' anagrams ARMY into MARY.
explanation.definitionFit: A vodka-and-tomato-juice mixed drink is named after a Tudor queen, making it a classic cocktail.

clue.text: Word in French, true, may be encountered around northern

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Word in French, true, may be encountered around northern', has no count and no definition: MOT around N plus REAL gives the letters, but the defining word (presumably 'city') is cut off, and no search found the full text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Word in French, true, may be encountered around northern

clue.text: Playwright making a person sick

parts.note: one can stand for a single unnamed individual, as in 'one does one's best'
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A dramatist whose plays make a person feel queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene O'Neill was an American playwright; 'making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill wrote Long Day's Journey into Night, so he is a famous dramatist.

clue.text: Sound of crying from some girl we muddled up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
only some of the letters of these words are taken, a run lying across them

explanation.surface: A girl and I got confused and heard a whimper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'muddled' looks like an anagram signal but is just a fodder word: 'some' takes LWEM from girL WE Muddled and 'up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To mewl is to whimper or cry feebly, like a baby or a kitten.

clue.text: Meat and a quantity of drink supplied by city

parts.note: liver is offal eaten as meat
a pool is a quantity of liquid gathered together, such as spilled drink

explanation.surface: A city's caterers providing offal and plenty to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supplied by' is a link between the wordplay and the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool is a major port city in north-west England.

clue.text: Wild cat showing exuberance, tearing head off

indicators.note: the first letter of the synonym is ripped away

parts.note: bounce is lively energy and exuberance

explanation.surface: A big cat full of high spirits ripping the head off its prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a wild cat of Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: Church decoration -have another try fitting in most of remainder

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
the word loses its last letter, leaving most of it

parts.note: the rest is what remains
to redo something is to do it again

explanation.surface: Someone redecorating a church who has to start again with leftover materials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fitting in' puts REDO inside RES, which is REST with 'most of' dropping its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A reredos is an ornamental screen behind a church altar, a piece of ecclesiastical decoration.

clue.text: Crooked relation, drug confiscated, facing a jury

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
something confiscated is taken away, so the drug's letter is removed

parts.note: E is the slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A bent relative has drugs seized and ends up in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confiscated' removes E (ecstasy) from RELATION, and 'Crooked' rearranges the remaining RLATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant on trial is having their case heard before a jury.

clue.text: … twelve people, ultimately, not an individual

parts.note: twelve o'clock midday is noon

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the final letter of people is taken

explanation.surface: Twelve people turn up, but in the end nobody in particular.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots link to the previous clue in print but carry no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying nobody at all is present means not a single individual.

clue.text: Crumbling wall obeys physical restriction

indicators.note: a crumbling wall falls apart, and so do these letters, which are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A wall falling down still obeys the laws of physics.
explanation.walkthrough: BOYLE'S LAW is the gas law stating that pressure and volume vary inversely at constant temperature: a physical law, here a 'restriction'.
explanation.definitionFit: A law of physics constrains how a gas behaves, so it can be called a physical restriction.

clue.text: Not sticking to schedule, like us in Tuscany?

definitions.meaning: British clocks run an hour later than Italian ones, so Britons in Tuscany are an hour off local time

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is whimsical: Italy keeps Central European Time, one hour ahead of the UK, so British visitors with unchanged watches are an hour slow.
explanation.definitionFit: Being late means lagging the clock, as British watches lag Italian clocks by an hour.

clue.text: Question of identity surrounds crooked steward in novel

indicators.note: one piece is placed around the other

parts.note: 'who?' is the question asked to learn someone's identity

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dishonest steward in a novel is questioned about who he really is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounds' puts WHO around ESTWARD, the anagram of STEWARD from 'crooked'. Westward Ho! is an 1855 novel by Charles Kingsley.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley's Westward Ho! is a Victorian adventure novel about Elizabethan seafarers.

clue.text: Use anti-ageing cream, perhaps, and attract attention

definitions.meaning: read literally, to strike at the wrinkles on one's forehead

explanation.surface: Someone whose wrinkle cream gets them noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a pun: 'lines' on the head are wrinkles, which anti-ageing cream attacks; 'and' links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: A story or person that becomes major news is suddenly in the public eye and draws attention.

clue.text: Was almost implicated in more aggravated trouble

indicators.note: being implicated in something is being caught up inside it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: someone hotter is more heated and angry

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A suspect almost dragged into an increasingly heated row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims WAS to WA, and 'implicated in' puts that inside HOTTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in hot water is an idiom for being in trouble.

clue.text: That place mostly in the grip of Scandinavian goddess of the polar regions?

indicators.note: held inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: the Norns are the goddesses of fate in Norse myth

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: there means that place

explanation.surface: A Norse goddess holding sway over the far north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts THERE to THER and 'in the grip of' puts it inside NORN. The question mark admits the definition is loose: only one polar region is northern.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic lies at the top of the globe, so things there are of the far north.

clue.text: Milan, city torn apart by aggressive attitude

indicators.note: a city torn apart is wrecked, and its letters are reassembled in another order

explanation.surface: Milan is a city ripped apart by belligerent protests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'torn apart' signals the anagram of MILAN and CITY; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Militancy is a combative, confrontational stance, especially in a political cause.

clue.text: Work party?

definitions.meaning: the British political party of the left

explanation.walkthrough: Labour is one of Britain's two main political parties.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour means toil, and it is also the name of a major UK political party.

clue.text: in sort of poll

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'in sort of poll', is cut short with no count: the answer suits 'straw poll', but the rest of the clue is missing and no search found it.

clue.text: I will take part in climbing holidays, showing mettle

indicators.note: to take part in something is to get inside it, so the letter goes inside
in a down clue, climbing means the letters are read upwards

parts.note: trips are short holidays

explanation.surface: I'll join climbing holidays, showing plenty of courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns TRIPS to SPIRT and 'take part in' puts I inside; 'will' and 'showing' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit is courage and determination, which is what mettle means.

clue.text: Shout loudly after six bowled with vigour?

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
to rant is to shout loudly and at length

explanation.surface: A fielder shouting loudly after six batsmen are bowled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts RANT after VI and B. The question mark notes the definition is an adjective phrase for a one-word adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Vibrant means full of energy and life, so it describes something done with vigour.

clue.text: Titanic ignoring a warning at sea

indicators.note: the letter is ignored, so it is left out

parts.note: avast is the sailor's call to stop

explanation.surface: The Titanic ignored a warning while at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' looks like the liner, but it is the adjective meaning huge.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic means gigantic, like the Titans of Greek myth, so enormous.

clue.text: Baron excited the girl with empty talk

parts.note: lit means aroused or excited, as in lit up
her refers to a girl

explanation.surface: A baron is so taken with a girl that he babbles nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' looks like an anagram signal but gives LIT; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To blither is to talk foolishly at length, which is idle chatter.

clue.text: Cricketers cracked

explanation.walkthrough: A batsman 'bats'; and 'bats' is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Batters bat in cricket, and being nuts or crazy is described as bats.

clue.text: It may accompany flesh (lip or cheek)

explanation.walkthrough: 'lip' and 'cheek' both mean insolence, and so does the answer; the brackets hide that lip and cheek are also flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: A condiment like gravy goes with meat, and insolent talk is called the same thing.

clue.text: Month including endlessly difficult time for the head of the family

indicators.note: one piece contains the other

parts.note: March is a month

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a trial is a hardship or difficult time

explanation.surface: A month of endless hardship for the head of the household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts TRIAL to TRIA and 'including' puts it inside MARCH; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A matriarch is the woman who rules a family or clan, its female head.
